completions.policy: Policy: Module dependency cycle (ARCH-CYCLE-001, version 2, severity high)

telemetry.accounting: SDK query-pipeline totals including cache input; cost estimate, not subscription billing

verdicts.reasoning: Both edges of the left<->right loop are `import type` declarations, which TypeScript erases at emit. No runtime require/ESM edge is produced, so there is no initialization-order hazard and no runtime coupling. Mutually recursive type definitions across two sibling type modules are an intended modeling pattern, and the policy explicitly exempts harmless type-only cycles. Note this is not a module-detection artifact: types/left and types/right are genuinely distinct modules, so the detected loop is real but benign. Residual caveat: under isolatedModules-style settings, or if either `import type` is later changed to a value import, this would become a live cycle; that is a lint-guard concern, not a current high-severity boundary violation.

All three edges are value imports (`import { inventory }`, `import { sales }`, `import { billing }`), which survive compilation and form a closed runtime dependency path across three distinct business-domain modules. This obstructs intended boundaries: billing, inventory and sales become one indivisible unit that cannot be built, tested or deployed independently, and whichever module is loaded first will observe partially-initialized bindings from the others (undefined-at-import-time, or TDZ errors for const/class bindings). Evidence supplies each edge of the closed path, so the witness is complete for the claimed cycle; per the scope note the true coupling may be broader, so the remediation should break the loop structurally (extract shared contracts downward or invert one edge behind an interface/event) rather than merely rerouting the single reported import.

completions.policy: Policy: Complex control flow (QUALITY-COMPLEXITY-001, version 1, severity medium)

telemetry.accounting: SDK query-pipeline totals including cache input; cost estimate, not subscription billing

verdicts.reasoning: The excerpt shows complexity 18 arising from four interleaved responsibilities in one function body: pricing/discount policy (VIP, country 'PE', imported, fragile/express surcharges), inventory mutation (decrementing stock, writing negative quantities for backorder), customer credit accounting (mutating customer.credit), and payment capture with retry/failure state (order.retry, order.failed, order.pending, order.blocked, order.manualReview, order.rejected). Nesting reaches five levels and the function mutates three caller-owned objects as side effects while also returning a computed total, so individual paths cannot be exercised in isolation. The catch block branching on customer.vip embeds business policy inside error handling. The function's own comment corroborates the mixing of concerns. This is a maintainability problem established by the evidence, remediable by extracting pricing, inventory reservation, and payment-outcome handling.

decodeProtocolTag is a flat, exhaustive protocol decoder: sixteen independent constant case arms each returning a single string, plus a default that throws on unknown tags. The complexity value of 17 is an artifact of counting case labels rather than of tangled logic. There is a single responsibility (tag to name), zero nesting, no side effects, no shared mutable state, and no cross-branch state a reader must track. This matches the intentional dispatch-table pattern the policy directs us to reject; the evidence establishes no maintainability problem, and converting it to a lookup map would lower the metric without improving clarity.
